title: The Kongo kingdom
question: How can we follow a kingdom beyond present borders?
standfirst: A capital now in Angola, Atlantic exchanges and rival powers: the Kongo kingdom requires a reading at several scales.

thesis.heading: A documented encounter, not a beginning

figures.claim: The arrival of Diogo Cão marks diplomatic contact with the Portuguese.
figures.provenance: The kingdom already exists; this date does not mark its foundation.

chapters.title: A capital and its networks
chapters.question: What does Mbanza Kongo represent?
chapters.standfirst: The city locates power without drawing an unchanging territory.

body.text: Mbanza Kongo, in present-day Angola, is the political and spiritual capital of a kingdom UNESCO dates from the fourteenth to the nineteenth century. Its remains bear witness to royal, religious and urban functions.
The Met exhibition distinguishes the kingdom from neighbouring formations such as Loango. Kongo works circulate between courts: cultural proximity alone does not establish shared sovereignty.

readings.label: The centre of power
readings.body: The heritage designation documents the capital and its transformations. The protected site does not define the historical boundaries of the kingdom.

readings.label: African diplomatic voices
readings.body: Surviving letters from Kongo rulers also let us read exchanges through their political and religious concerns.

illustration.alt: Brass crucifix with a central Christ and several smaller figures.
illustration.caption: Kongo crucifix, sixteenth–seventeenth century. A local reinterpretation, not a royal portrait.

chapters.title: Ruptures and transformations
chapters.question: Does the death of a king end an entire society?
chapters.standfirst: Political history continues through changes of power.

body.text: In 1665, António I dies at Mbwila, facing Portuguese forces. The Met chronology presents the battle as a rupture in central authority. It does not mark the disappearance of Kongo populations.
Cécile Fromont considers internal conflicts alongside the expanding Atlantic slave trade. A single-cause account obscures their interactions and the unequal choices available to participants.

readings.label: A military rupture
readings.body: The battle provides a dated landmark for understanding political fragmentation rather than a peaceful succession of reigns.

readings.label: Active religious transformations
readings.body: The crucifix shown here demonstrates Kongo artists adapting Christian forms. Adoption is more than copying.

gaps.reason: This dossier does not reconstruct annual kingdom boundaries or a complete list of rulers. Connections to present-day countries are reading landmarks.
